name: Lemon juice / baking soda on scars
lead: Applying lemon juice, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) or a paste of the two to scars is a do-it-yourself practice that circulates as a way to lighten and smooth marks left by acne, injuries or surgery. The idea, as practitioners describe it, is that lemon juice's acidity fades dark marks and that baking soda's grit exfoliates raised or rough skin, giving a more even complexion and a less visible scar.

No clinical studies of the practice itself were found. Reference material on related topics describes how scars are classified and treated in clinics, what citrus juice can do to skin in sunlight, and how popular home remedies built on baking soda and lemon juice have been characterized in the medical literature.[1][2][3][4]

The most documented risk is phytophotodermatitis, a reaction in which plant compounds called furanocoumarins on the skin react to UVA light, producing redness, burning and blisters, usually followed by dark pigmented marks that can last for years.[2][3]

chain: Acidic juice and an abrasive powder applied to a scar
Scar blends in more with surrounding skin
angle.text: Practitioners apply the ingredients to lighten dark scar marks and to roughly smooth the skin surface so that a scar is less noticeable. The aim is a more even skin tone, achieved with inexpensive kitchen ingredients.

paras: The practice uses common kitchen ingredients. Lemon juice is acidic, and sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution and has mild abrasive properties.[5] Variants include juice alone, baking soda mixed with water, or both combined into a paste that is left on the skin for a period and rinsed off.

Scars take several forms. Hypertrophic and keloid scars are raised, atrophic scars (common after acne or chickenpox) are sunken, and many scars also carry a color change.[1] The home remedy is usually discussed in connection with the color and surface texture of such marks.

For comparison, the Wikipedia scar article lists silicone products, lasers (ablative lasers are described as best suited to atrophic and acne scars), corticosteroid injections for keloid and hypertrophic scars, and massage, with a weak evidence base reported for several of these. It also notes that some forms of vitamin C may fade dark pigment associated with scars.[1]

Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with furanocoumarins, found in limes and other plants, and then UVA exposure. Reactions begin within about 24 to 48 hours and heal over several weeks, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation typically remains, in some cases for several years and often more intensely in skin of colour.[2][3] DermNet describes lime as the best-known citrus trigger and does not mention lemon specifically; Wikipedia lists citrus including lime among triggers.[2][3] Dermatology guidance for the reaction includes cool compresses, avoiding the plant and using high-UVA sun protection.[3]

Sodium bicarbonate is listed as causing serious eye irritation.[5] A 2021 narrative review in Biochemical Pharmacology noted that claims that baking soda, lemon juice and apple cider vinegar are cures for a wide range of conditions circulate widely online, while describing acid-base therapies with established uses in specific medical conditions.[4]

refs.title: The therapeutic importance of acid-base balance

card.summary: Kitchen-ingredient scar remedy; no studies found, and citrus juice is a known cause of light-triggered skin reactions.
card.aka: DIY scar exfoliation, lemon and bicarbonate paste
card.note: Citrus juice plus sunlight can cause blistering and long-lasting dark marks (phytophotodermatitis).

quick.overview:
This home remedy involves rubbing lemon juice, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), or a mix of the two on scars, with the idea of lightening or exfoliating them.

No studies were found testing this practice for scars. Separate reference material documents that citrus juice can cause skin reactions with sunlight.
quick.mechanism: Believers' reasoning typically centres on lemon juice's acidity as a lightener and baking soda's abrasiveness as an exfoliant. This reasoning is not supported by published trials in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that follows contact with plant furanocoumarins (found in citrus such as lime) and UV-A light, producing redness, burning and blisters within about 48 hours, and pigment marks that can persist for years. Sodium bicarbonate is listed as causing serious eye irritation.
